instructions.content: A plain WebFetch or curl of the comparison page returns an empty table because the page is rendered client-side. Read the published data/context-reduction-tools.json dataset with the fetch script instead.

layers[].cardinality is the load-bearing field: pick-one/either-or means install exactly one tool for that layer, stackable means several may coexist, install-both is zero-config and always-on, reference is a curated list and not itself installable.
Workflow step 1: fetch the dataset first and note meta.last_updated, so any finding is dated against a known snapshot.
Workflow step 2: run collect-active-tools.sh to enumerate what is actually active at both project and global scope, including tools wired as raw hook binaries, not just MCP server registrations.
Workflow step 3: mapping an active tool to a dataset id needs judgement, not string matching. A hook command's path can map to a dataset id that shares little or no substring with it.

Workflow step 4: for every pick-one/either-or layer, count active tools mapped to it. More than one is a redundancy finding, cited against that layer's cardinality and note field, not against personal preference.

Workflow step 4: a tool with verdict.decision of drop is a removal finding on its own. A tool with verdict watch and activityStatus.band dormant is a staleness finding to note, not a standalone removal recommendation.
Workflow step 4: a layer with a curatedPick and zero active coverage is an optional-add note, not a finding, because absence is not a defect.

Workflow step 4: check permission allowlist entries (mcp__<server>__* prefixes) against the actual mcpServers registrations for that server name in both project and global .mcp.json. Allowlisted but unregistered is a phantom-tool finding, since any rule mandating that tool is currently unenforceable.
Workflow step 4: if a rule file mandates a tool, verify that the tool it names actually resolves to something active. A mandate pointing at a phantom or absent tool is worth surfacing on its own.
Workflow step 5: report findings as a list and let the user decide what to action. Do not edit global config as part of running the audit.
Workflow step 6: file findings via the create-context-file skill, then regenerate the index via the context-index skill. Findings left only in the chat response do not survive a session reset.
Mindset: the dataset is a snapshot with a stated freshness date. Treat star counts and watch-tier verdicts as time-bound, not permanent.

Mindset: a tool being active and a tool being wired in are different things. Hooks, MCP registration, and permission allowlists can drift independently, which is exactly how a phantom-tool finding happens.
Mindset: redundancy findings are about layer cardinality, not personal preference. Cite the layer's cardinality and note field as the reasoning, never that something merely seems duplicative.
Mindset: default to reporting. Treat global-config edits as requiring explicit user sign-off every time, not just the first time a redundancy is found.

NEVER treat an empty table returned from fetching the comparison page directly as evidence that there is no data. The fetch tool never runs the page's client-side rendering, so the raw HTML genuinely has no rows regardless of what the page shows in a browser.
NEVER treat a tool's absence from any .mcp.json as proof it is inactive. Some dataset tools run as hook-invoked CLI binaries with no MCP server registration at all.
NEVER edit global Claude Code config as part of running this audit. Those files apply to every project on the machine, so an unrequested edit has a blast radius far beyond the project being audited.
